paragraphs.text: Hiring your first member of staff is one of the biggest steps a small business owner will take. Overnight, you stop being responsible only for yourself and become responsible for someone else's income, safety and working conditions. This guide from the Eastbrook Business Advice Office sets out the main tasks involved and the order in which to tackle them. It is not a substitute for professional legal advice, and because employment rules differ from one country to another, you should always check the details that apply where you trade. Our advisers offer free one-to-one sessions every Tuesday morning for anyone who wants to talk through their plans.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Before you write an advertisement, ask yourself whether you genuinely need an employee. If the extra work comes in short bursts, a freelancer paid by the job may be a cheaper and more flexible solution. If you decide that a permanent role makes sense, put together a job description that sets out the main duties, the expected hours and the rate of pay. This document will shape your advertisement, guide your interviews and later form the basis of the contract, so it is worth taking time over it. Then work out what the post will really cost. Wages are only part of the picture: you may also have to pay employer contributions to the state, fund paid holidays and buy equipment or uniforms. Marguerite Oyelowo, who has advised local firms at our office for over a decade, tells clients to add about a fifth to the basic wage when they draw up their budget. 'Owners who plan around the wage alone are often caught out by the extra costs within the first few months,' she says.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Once the budget is settled, deal with the official side. In many countries you must register as an employer with the tax authority before the first payday, because you will be responsible for deducting income tax from your employee's wages and passing it on. You will also need a way of running payroll; many small firms use inexpensive software, while others pay an accountant to handle it. Also find out whether the law requires you to hold insurance that covers claims from staff who are injured or fall ill because of their work. In some places this cover is compulsory from the day your first employee starts, and the fines for not having it can be heavy.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: With the paperwork under way, you can start recruiting. Advertise in places your candidate is likely to look, and ask every applicant the same core questions at interview so that you can compare them fairly. Before making a firm offer, check that your chosen candidate has the legal right to work in the country. This usually means seeing original documents, such as a passport, in the person's presence and keeping a dated copy on file. Photocopies or photographs sent by email are not enough. It is also sensible to contact at least one previous employer for a reference, although a reference should never replace your own judgement.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Your new employee is entitled to clear written terms. In many countries these must be provided on or before their first day, not weeks later once they have settled in. As a minimum, the document should state the job title, pay, working hours, holiday entitlement and how much notice either side must give to end the arrangement. If you include a probation period, say how long it lasts and what will happen at the end of it.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The first week deserves careful planning. A proper induction should cover health and safety procedures, the location of first-aid equipment, how to deal with customers and, above all, whom to ask when something is unclear. Sanjay Whitlock, who runs a bakery on Mill Street, admits he got this wrong. 'My first assistant was simply handed an apron and told to get on with it,' he recalls. 'She left after three weeks.' Since then he has used a one-page checklist for every new starter, and his second recruit has now been with him for four years.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Finally, keep accurate records of the hours your employee works, the pay they receive and any holiday they take, as you may be asked to produce these. Arrange a short review at the end of the probation period, and after that make time for regular conversations rather than waiting for problems to build up. Staff who feel listened to are more likely to stay, and replacing someone usually costs more than keeping them.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Taking On Your First Employee

A. Hiring your first member of staff is one of the biggest steps a small business owner will take. Overnight, you stop being responsible only for yourself and become responsible for someone else's income, safety and working conditions. This guide from the Eastbrook Business Advice Office sets out the main tasks involved and the order in which to tackle them. It is not a substitute for professional legal advice, and because employment rules differ from one country to another, you should always check the details that apply where you trade. Our advisers offer free one-to-one sessions every Tuesday morning for anyone who wants to talk through their plans.

B. Before you write an advertisement, ask yourself whether you genuinely need an employee. If the extra work comes in short bursts, a freelancer paid by the job may be a cheaper and more flexible solution. If you decide that a permanent role makes sense, put together a job description that sets out the main duties, the expected hours and the rate of pay. This document will shape your advertisement, guide your interviews and later form the basis of the contract, so it is worth taking time over it. Then work out what the post will really cost. Wages are only part of the picture: you may also have to pay employer contributions to the state, fund paid holidays and buy equipment or uniforms. Marguerite Oyelowo, who has advised local firms at our office for over a decade, tells clients to add about a fifth to the basic wage when they draw up their budget. 'Owners who plan around the wage alone are often caught out by the extra costs within the first few months,' she says.

C. Once the budget is settled, deal with the official side. In many countries you must register as an employer with the tax authority before the first payday, because you will be responsible for deducting income tax from your employee's wages and passing it on. You will also need a way of running payroll; many small firms use inexpensive software, while others pay an accountant to handle it. Also find out whether the law requires you to hold insurance that covers claims from staff who are injured or fall ill because of their work. In some places this cover is compulsory from the day your first employee starts, and the fines for not having it can be heavy.

D. With the paperwork under way, you can start recruiting. Advertise in places your candidate is likely to look, and ask every applicant the same core questions at interview so that you can compare them fairly. Before making a firm offer, check that your chosen candidate has the legal right to work in the country. This usually means seeing original documents, such as a passport, in the person's presence and keeping a dated copy on file. Photocopies or photographs sent by email are not enough. It is also sensible to contact at least one previous employer for a reference, although a reference should never replace your own judgement.

E. Your new employee is entitled to clear written terms. In many countries these must be provided on or before their first day, not weeks later once they have settled in. As a minimum, the document should state the job title, pay, working hours, holiday entitlement and how much notice either side must give to end the arrangement. If you include a probation period, say how long it lasts and what will happen at the end of it.

F. The first week deserves careful planning. A proper induction should cover health and safety procedures, the location of first-aid equipment, how to deal with customers and, above all, whom to ask when something is unclear. Sanjay Whitlock, who runs a bakery on Mill Street, admits he got this wrong. 'My first assistant was simply handed an apron and told to get on with it,' he recalls. 'She left after three weeks.' Since then he has used a one-page checklist for every new starter, and his second recruit has now been with him for four years.

G. Finally, keep accurate records of the hours your employee works, the pay they receive and any holiday they take, as you may be asked to produce these. Arrange a short review at the end of the probation period, and after that make time for regular conversations rather than waiting for problems to build up. Staff who feel listened to are more likely to stay, and replacing someone usually costs more than keeping them.
